cards.explanation: The answer is that he tells him to turn in an account because he cannot be manager any longer. The rich man says, "What is this I hear about you? Turn in an account of your management, for you cannot be manager any longer." (Luke 16:2) He asks for the books and tells the manager the job is ending. Basically, "hand me the paperwork," friends.

The answer is False, friends. The manager says, "I am too weak to dig and too ashamed to beg." (Luke 16:3) He names both options and crosses them off in one sentence. That's a man with a lot of thinking to do, and he's about to do it.

The plan is so that people will welcome him into their homes. The manager says, "I know what I will do so that after my removal from management, people will welcome me into their homes." (Luke 16:4) He's already planning for after his removal. Say what you want about him, friends, the man does not sit around waiting.

The answer is to sit down quickly and write fifty. The manager tells the first debtor, "Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write fifty." (Luke 16:6) A hundred measures of olive oil becomes fifty. Notice the "quickly," too, bakers. This man is not asking for a second opinion.

The answer is eighty. The second debtor owes a hundred measures of wheat, and the manager says, "Take your bill and write eighty…" (Luke 16:7) Each debtor gets a different number, friends. Fifty for the first, eighty for the second.

Plot twist, friends: the master commends him for acting shrewdly. "The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly." (Luke 16:8) A pat on the back is not what I'd have expected from that master. The text still calls him the dishonest manager, so the shrewdness is what gets commended.

The answer is True. Jesus says, "For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light." (Luke 16:8) It's a comparison, friends, and the sons of light come out second. I think that's worth a quiet moment of thinking.

The answer is to make friends for themselves. Jesus says, "I tell you, use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves…" (Luke 16:9) The manager in the story used his master's bills to make friends, and now Jesus talks about worldly wealth the same way. Money in your hands can be put to work for people, bakers.

The answer is True. Jesus says to use worldly wealth to make friends "…so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings." (Luke 16:9) Notice the "…when it is gone…" friends. The wealth is gone, and the dwellings Jesus names are eternal.

The answer is False, friends. Jesus says, "Whoever is faithful with very little will also be faithful with much, and whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much." (Luke 16:10) So being dishonest with little doesn't prepare you to be honest with much. It goes the other direction.

The answer is true riches. Jesus asks, "So if you have not been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches?" (Luke 16:11) He puts worldly wealth and true riches in the same question, friends. The thing to fill in is "true riches."

The word that fills the blank is "own." Jesus asks, "And if you have not been faithful with the belongings of another, who will give you belongings of your own?" (Luke 16:12) He sets belongings of another next to belongings of your own, bakers.

The answer is False, friends. Jesus says, "No servant can serve two masters. Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other." (Luke 16:13) He lays out two outcomes, and equal love for both isn't one of them.

The two masters are God and money. Jesus ends with, "You cannot serve both God and money." (Luke 16:13) The whole passage has been talking about wealth, friends, and this is where He lands it. Two masters, and those are the two.
